Harden
HAR-den
v.
Old English heardian, from heard (hard). Renders the Hebrew qāshāh, “to be hard, stiff,” chāzaq, “to make strong, harden,” and kābad (hiphil), “to make heavy”; and the Greek sklērunō, “to harden,” and pōroō, “to petrify, render insensible.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To harden, in Scripture, is to render a heart unresponsive, callous, or insensible to God’s Word, Spirit, and providence—and the verb is used both of God’s judicial hardening of the rebel and of the rebel’s own self-hardening against grace. The Pharaoh narrative of Exodus is the textbook case: Pharaoh hardens his own heart (Ex 8:15, 32; 9:34), and God hardens Pharaoh’s heart (Ex 9:12; 10:1, 20; 11:10); the two stand together without contradiction, and Paul appeals to the same case in Romans 9 to set forth God’s sovereignty over the hard heart: therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth. The biblical anatomy of hardening is sober. It is rarely a sudden act and almost always a process: the conscience repeatedly resists known truth, the affections cool toward God, the will refuses to yield, and the heart over time grows callous to what once pricked it. Hebrews 3–4 sets the warning at its most pastoral pitch: today if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness; the writer charges his hearers to exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin. The hardening is the soul’s loss of softness to the Spirit’s touch—a deafening of the inward ear, a calcification of the inward eye, an unresponsive heart where there was once a tender one. Its end is the awful judicial reprobation in which God hands the hardened soul over to its chosen darkness: Romans 1 thrice repeats God gave them up. Its remedy is repentance under the Word and the breaking of the soul before the cross, where God promises to take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and give you an heart of flesh. To hear of hardening and to feel any softening at the warning is itself a token of grace; to hear and be unmoved is the very symptom the warning addresses.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HARDEN as to make hard or harder; to confirm in effrontery, in wickedness, or in obstinacy; to render insensible or unfeeling.

expand to see more

HARDEN, v.t. — 1. To make hard or more hard; to make firm or compact. 2. To confirm in effrontery; to make impudent. 3. To confirm in wickedness, obstinacy, or any evil course; as, to harden the heart. 4. To render insensible or unfeeling; as, to harden the conscience.

HARDENING, ppr. — Making hard or more hard; making obdurate, unfeeling, or obstinate; confirming in effrontery or in wickedness.

📖 Key Scripture

Hebrews 3:13 — "But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin."

Hebrews 3:15 — "While it is said, To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts, as in the provocation."

Exodus 9:12 — "And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he hearkened not unto them; as the LORD had spoken unto Moses."

Romans 9:18 — "Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The doctrine of hardening is corrupted by the therapeutic age’s denial that there is such a thing as a calloused soul—every soul is treated as soft, tender, and merely needing more affirmation—and by the inverse error that treats hardening as so total and judicial that it removes responsibility from the one whose own daily resistance to God’s Word produced it.

expand to see more

The therapeutic age cannot recognize hardening because it does not believe in the moral diagnosis on which hardening rests. Where Scripture says the resisted Word, the indulged sin, and the rejected Spirit produce a calloused heart, the therapeutic register insists that all hearts remain tender beneath the surface and that the appearance of hardness is only unmet need. The result is pastoral malpractice. The hardened are told they are wounded; the calloused conscience is treated as a tender one; the warning passages of Hebrews 3–4 are read as encouragement and never as the sober rebuke they are; and the very softness the warning aims to recover is forfeited because the diagnosis the warning depends on has been denied. Recover the biblical diagnosis, and the warnings recover their force: today, if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.

The opposite corruption removes responsibility by treating hardening as a fixed judicial act in which the person became merely a passive object of God’s reprobating decree. The Pharaoh narrative refuses both errors. Pharaoh hardens his own heart and God hardens Pharaoh’s heart; the two stand together throughout the chapters; the self-hardening is real and culpable, and the divine hardening is real and sovereign. The pastoral application follows: every act of resisting known truth, of indulging known sin, of refusing the Spirit’s touch, contributes to the soul’s present softness or hardness; and the sober use of the warning is to keep today in view—to soften under the Word in this hour, before the deceitfulness of sin works the calcification it always works when given time.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qāshāh (to be hard), chāzaq (to make strong), kābad (hiphil—to make heavy); Greek sklērunō (to harden) and pōroō (to petrify, render insensible)—the calcification of the heart against God’s Word, Spirit, and providence.

expand to see more

Hebrew qāshāh (H7185) — to be hard, stiff, stubborn.

Hebrew chāzaq (H2388) — to be strong, to harden (used of Pharaoh’s heart).

Greek sklērunō (G4645) — to harden (Heb 3:8, 13, 15; Acts 19:9; Rom 9:18).

Greek pōroō (G4456) — to petrify, render insensible (Mark 6:52; John 12:40; Rom 11:7).

Usage

"Hardening is rarely sudden and almost always a process—the conscience that repeatedly resists known truth becomes the conscience that no longer feels the touch."

"Pharaoh hardens his own heart and God hardens Pharaoh’s heart—both true, both stated in the same chapters, and both refused by the therapeutic and the fatalistic corruptions alike."

"Today, if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts—the warning’s force is preserved only where the diagnosis it depends on is preserved."
